# Question

How does a small mitochondrial genome support a much larger protein machine network?

# Browser notes

Record a genome accession/version, one drug-target structure and the transcript-specific LMNA variant you investigated. Include the date viewed and distinguish a database annotation from a measurement.

# Data

```{r fetch-data}
records <- fetch_organelle_data(use_snapshot)
genes <- records$genes
proteins <- records$proteins
head(genes)
```

Data mode: `r records$mode`. Retrieval date: `r records$retrieved`.
UniProtKB release: `r records$release`.

- NCBI request: `r records$ncbi_url`
- UniProt request: `r records$uniprot_url`
- RefSeq genome: NC_012920.1, 16,569 bp. NCBI data reuse policy: <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/home/about/policies/>.
- UniProt data: CC BY 4.0, <https://www.uniprot.org/help/license>.

Live requests are cached in `data/` under the retrieval date; re-knitting on that date reuses them. Snapshot mode requires the two downloaded CSVs and makes no web requests. The provided helper parses CDS/tRNA/rRNA features and matches them to gene features; coordinates are 1-based and inclusive. Overlapping genes remain separate features.

# Interpretation

Write a results paragraph with at least one inline R value. Explain why a mitochondrial disease can be caused by a nuclear gene.

A map of annotations shows where genes lie; it does not measure how strongly each gene is expressed. A CDS feature and a gene feature must not be counted twice. Overlaps mean summing feature lengths does not give the fraction of unique bases covered.
